paragraphs: In Chang’an, the first people to sense that something had gone wrong along the Huai were the sellers of horse fodder.

Late that spring, the proprietor of a fodder shop in the Eastern Market went three days without a shipment of alfalfa from Hedong. No convoy had been robbed, and the official road was open. The carter who brought word said that the military administration had diverted all the fodder; even the allotment meant for the post horses at Luoyang was in arrears. Beneath a shed more than half empty, the proprietor cursed a while. Then officials arrived to ask whether he would sell the rest of his stock to the court.
Two streets away, on Vermilion Bird Avenue, people were still telling tales of Xiangyang in the winehouses.

“General Murong broke across the Han River with a single charge!” The storyteller struck his bamboo clappers, and his audience roared approval. The fall of the city, more than half a year past, was still keeping many taverns in business. A drinker pushed his teacup south across the table: there it went, over the Huai and straight to Jiankang. No one asked how many crossings lay beneath that cup, how many marshes, how much mud deep enough to swallow a wagon axle.

By the time Fu Hong saw the first fodder shortfall at the Secretariat, Zhu Xu had been a guest at the Court for State Guests for months. The crown prince ordered the deficit copied onto another sheet, beside figures showing the shortfall in provisions during the previous year’s Xiangyang campaign. He remembered the bodies left unburied outside the city walls, and the limits on further campaigning that Fu Jian had written in his own hand.
The trouble had begun the previous autumn.

In the first days after news of victory at Xiangyang reached the capital, the ritual officers were busy giving thanks at the ancestral temple, and the courtiers were busy drafting rewards. Many civilian wagons requisitioned in Nanyang were still stranded by the Han River, and the army’s grain accounts had yet to balance, but fresh memorials were already reaching Fu Jian’s desk. Some urged him to take Jiangling while victory favored them; others begged for a forward command north of the Huai. Peng Chao, a frontier general who claimed to know the Huai country intimately, offered to lead seventy thousand men south by several routes, taking forts and cutting the Jin army’s waterways.
Fu Rong spread out Peng Chao’s map. The first thing he examined was not a city.
“Which roads will the grain wagons use?”
Peng Chao’s deputy pointed to a long line of ink. “The commanderies of Yan and Yu will supply us. From Pengcheng we distribute the loads.”
“Why is there no river marked along this stretch?”
“It’s shallow. The wagons can ford it.”

Fu Rong called for the previous year’s flood register and pushed over the page recording the rains. It listed one bridge destroyed, two embankments breached, and two hundred shi of grain abandoned by drivers trying to save their draft animals. The deputy glanced at it but insisted that last year’s flooding had been exceptional and could not stand for every season.

Murong Chui stood behind the gathering without speaking for a long while. Only when Fu Pi asked his opinion did he approach the map and set a copper paperweight, of the sort used in army tents, where the waterways crossed.
“There is no room here to deploy cavalry. If the Jin refuse to come ashore, where exactly do we chase them?”
“Take the crossings, and they’ll have to come,” Fu Pi said.
Murong Chui shook his head. “There may be ten crossings. There are only two or three roads a grain wagon can travel. The crossings may not be what the enemy intends to strike.”

Yao Chang was now Minister of Ceremonies, with no authority to deploy troops in council. From his place among those attending, he spoke deliberately. “If Qin sits still for months, the Jin will build more boats and strengthen their stockades. An opportunity in war does not wait. If we take only the north bank of the Huai and leave the Yangtze untouched, what harm is there in trying?”

Fu Rong turned his eyes toward him and said nothing. He had heard how lightly Yao Chang used the word *trying*. In the council hall, a war was just a word or two. Out in the provinces it meant tearing houses down for boat planking, conscripting laborers, feeding the autumn harvest to the horses.

Fu Jian granted Peng Chao’s request, but dictated a very precise edict. The eastern force was limited to seventy thousand men; no large army was to be moved privately from Guanzhong or the lands north of the Yellow River. If a reliable supply route could not be established within three months, the troops must return to their former defenses. No inhabitants of newly occupied forts were to be requisitioned without authorization. Fu Rong asked that the date of withdrawal be added at the end, and Fu Jian wrote it himself. Before the ink had dried, Peng Chao’s deputy was prostrate on the floor, thanking his sovereign.
No one foresaw that the orders would first lose their force while the army was still winning.

The first victory came at an earthen fort north of the Huai that had lain neglected for years. Its Jin garrison numbered only a few dozen and withdrew at the approach of Qin troops. A second dispatch reported two small crossings taken and more than seventy boats of assorted sizes captured. A third announced that the outer works of Pengcheng had fallen, and enclosed a little Jin banner, its corner scorched by smoke. At court the ministers congratulated one another over the banner. Fu Jian smiled too, and asked whether the army might move just a little farther south before the waters rose.
That little farther meant thirty li at first, then two more river stockades.

At the front, no one wanted to be the first to retreat. Every newly captured fort needed a garrison, every boat a guard; each time a grain convoy crossed one river, another detachment had to receive it beyond. Peng Chao’s orders went south one after another, written on silk, while the grain wagons moved more and more slowly. Fodder ran short even before rice. Warhorses tethered to the embankments gnawed at roots, their ribs showing through their hides. One soldier went out in the dark to fetch water at the edge of a marsh. Next morning they carried him back from the reeds, burning with fever.

At first the Jin scarcely showed themselves. By day there were only a few fishing boats, their rowers wearing straw rain capes and hats, hovering far out near the reeds. At night a granary might suddenly catch fire; a wooden bridge repaired only yesterday might be missing two beams by morning. Qin horsemen would charge out, their hooves crushing the pale reeds, and reach the water in time to see narrow boats slipping into a bend of the river. Before their archers could draw, the boats were gone.

In a fury, Peng Chao had a grain officer bound beneath a flagpole and demanded to know why only one hundred and ninety shi had arrived out of five hundred. Standing in the rain, the officer answered that wagons had overturned in ditches, civilian porters had cut into sacks to steal food, and three separate camps had intercepted loads with official orders. Every one of those orders bore a genuine seal.
Peng Chao did not behead him. He had him untied and ordered him to make the journey again.

Once a woman carrying a child came to Peng Chao’s tent. Her husband had been assigned as a boat steersman, promised release after two trips with army grain. More than forty days had passed. She could not read military papers; all she had was a little length of hemp rope he had left her, with a knot boatmen tied to recognize their own craft. An officer told her he might have gone to the forward camp and sent her to the next crossing. There they pointed farther south: grain boats were being escorted there too.

Holding her child, she followed the embankment until dusk and finally sat beside a broken boat. A row of knots hung along its gunwale. She felt them one by one, but none had the familiar turn. She did not know whether her husband had been seized by Jin soldiers or gone to the bottom of the river. The night wind made her child cry with cold. She begged a nearby soldier for hot water, and he ladled out half a spoonful of thin gruel from his pot. The following day he received ten strokes for giving away army provisions.
Peng Chao never heard of it. In the report submitted by the military administration, the whole incident left only one line: *Unauthorized use of army grain; punishment administered.*
It was at this point that Xie Xuan arrived in Guangling.

For his first three days in command he led no sortie beyond the walls. Instead he summoned boatmen who knew the Huai’s tributaries. An old helmsman, his face split by wind cracks, turned the water chart over and pointed to a stain on its back. “An old river used to run here. When it’s dry, an ox cart can pass. When the floodwater comes down from upstream, it’s a dead end.” A clerk, offended by the dirty map, wanted to make a clean copy; Xie Xuan told him not to rub the stain away yet.
“Where the stain lies, that is where the water goes?”
“Water remembers its old course. It doesn’t follow an official map,” the boatman said.
Xie Xuan copied those words beneath his orders.

Many of the Beifu soldiers were refugees from the north. Some had once ridden horses beyond the Yellow River and later begged for food along the banks of the Huai. Xie Xuan picked men who knew the channels for his boat crews, set the bowmen to guard the embankments, and drilled the others in night crossings again and again in small detachments. When asked why he did not march to recover the little towns, he answered, “If we scatter our men among the towns, who will watch Qin’s grain on the river?”

The Jin army’s first great victory came at an abandoned river stockade. More than three thousand Qin vanguard troops arrived to find the cooking fires still warm and half a mooring rope lying on the ground. Their commander ordered them inside to rest the horses. By dusk the sky had darkened, and rainwater from several days upstream came rushing down. The river swelled sharply. Jin troops had removed the middle section of a shallow bridge in advance and held the narrow road to the high embankment, firing from the side channels by torchlight. Qin soldiers hurried to leave their camp, but heavy wagons blocked the gate. Some stripped off armor and waded out. Others led horses toward the crossing; one frightened horse overturned two rafts carrying men.

Two days later, Peng Chao counted his men on the north bank. Of more than three thousand, only some twelve hundred had returned to their units. Not every missing man was dead, but discarded armor lay for half a li across the mud. The commander was stripped of his post and held to answer for the defeat. That night Peng Chao did not eat supper; he used the point of his knife to scratch new lines of march across the map.
Another fortnight passed. Then came the true disaster.

There was mist over the rivers that morning. Twenty thousand Qin vanguard troops held the high ground on the south bank, their grain camp on the north, connected by three floating bridges. Xie Xuan would not meet them head-on in open country. He sent light craft downstream by night to sever the piles anchoring the bridges; he also ordered watermen to open an old weir on a branch channel that had held back the water. No towering wave arrived overnight. Instead the river crept higher, first over the grass beside the bridges, then beneath the timber rafts, until ropes pegged to the banks drew taut and groaned.

By the time the bridge guards noticed, the first pontoon bridge had twisted halfway out of line. The alarm reached the forward camp and was taken for an enemy attack; armored men hurried to the embankment. By the time it reached the rear camp, the report had become a warning that the vanguard was trying to seize the bridges. Both banks struggled to send men across. The narrow spans filled with horsemen, baggage wagons, and infantry carrying shields. When the last great cable snapped, a raft with wagon wheels aboard lurched into the river, and dozens of men fell from the bridge together.

Still Xie Xuan did not sound the general advance. He set his boats above the crossing and his archers at the two tracks leading to the shallows, then waited for the forward camp to unravel. By the second night, some Qin soldiers were slaughtering their horses for food. On the third day the commander on the south bank ordered a breakout across the shallows. The first men into the river actually reached the far bank; those behind began jostling to follow. The riverbed was soft with silt. The front ranks stood fast with shields raised, while men in armor behind them sank into the mud. Then officers who had fled to the north bank shouted that the Jin had captured the grain camp. All order vanished.

Xie Xuan sent his troops to bar the retreat along the high ground. Men in the water threw away their helmets to stay afloat. Some were pulled out by comrades; others clung to bridge timbers and floated away downstream. Jin boats too were overturned by arrows and crossbow bolts from the bank. The armies fought in the mist until banners were indistinguishable. Near noon the Qin troops on the south bank finally forced open an escape route, but those who came out could no longer be called an army formation.

The mudflats were strewn with discarded armor and overturned grain wagons. No one could yet count the killed, the drowned, the captured, and the scattered. Of the twenty thousand vanguard troops, fewer than half returned to their units. Peng Chao still commanded the main body, but his food was gone and he could not rescue the men across the river. He could only gather survivors as he retreated north, abandoning heavy crossbows and several hundred horses too exhausted to walk. Some refused to leave wounded comrades, unloading weapons from their wagons to make room for men. Others deserted in the disorder. An officer called names in the mud, a third time, with no answer.
When the report of defeat reached Chengming Hall, Fu Jian’s first question was, “How many are missing?”
The reporting officer swallowed. “The camps are scattered too far apart. We have not yet been able to verify the number.”
“And the grain?”
“From the north bank to the forward camp, only two or three loads in ten arrived.”

Some in the hall urgently demanded reinforcements to wipe away Peng Chao’s disgrace. Another agreed, arguing that if Murong Chui took elite cavalry east, he could force Xie Xuan into battle. Fu Pi rose as well and asked to lead the old Xiangyang troops to the Huai in person.

Fu Rong took out two grain registers and placed them on the imperial desk. One was Peng Chao’s account, the other the record kept by the convoy officers along the road. The edges of the paper were filthy black, but the discrepancy could still be calculated.
“Your Majesty, I ask you to look at these two first.”

Fu Jian opened them. The first said the camps had provisions for another twenty days. The second recorded only six. Peng Chao had not openly told a lie to his sovereign: he had added together the grain in the storehouses, grain still on the road, and grain promised but not yet dispatched. Six days' food had become twenty on paper. Fu Jian read a long time, then set the two registers side by side.

Murong Chui stepped forward. “I can retake a stockade we have lost, Your Majesty. But if three hundred thousand troops are crowded into the lands south of the Huai, I cannot tell you how much grain they will consume each day. If we march now, I fear it is the convoy men who will suffer defeat first.”
“You too would have me withdraw?” Fu Jian asked.
“Yes.”
Fu Pi’s eyes were red. “Father, if we retreat this once, all under Heaven will know that Qin fears Xie Xuan.”
Fu Jian looked up at him. “All under Heaven knows already.”
He spoke so quietly that Fu Pi had no reply.

Fu Jian ordered Peng Chao back to the old line. The wounded were to go first, the rest to march north by separate camps, and no one was to seize grain from the people along the way. Officers who had crossed the authorized boundary were to be detained and investigated; Peng Chao was to surrender command and stand trial. The Secretariat was ordered to send men from camp to camp to verify the killed and wounded. No soldier entered merely as “missing” could be struck from the rolls without an attempt to find him. When the first withdrawal edict was issued, trophies from Xiangyang still hung outside the old palace gate. The victory banner had faded. Wind passed through the holes in its cloth, exposing the frayed edges within.

Weeks later the defeated troops reached Luoyang. People stood along the roadside, some offering water. There were no cheers. Two soldiers carried a dead comrade down from a wagon on a pair of door panels and asked where they could lay him temporarily. A gate clerk brought a blank name board and told them to write his name. The two men carrying him began to argue over whether his surname was He or another He written with a different character. He had been transferred from another unit, and his registration had not yet arrived.

At the reception camp outside Luoyang, clerks sent by Fu Hong wrote down names from dawn until dusk. Some men could give their home districts but not the numbers of their units; others remembered a commander’s nickname but did not know the name on his official papers. A thin Qiang soldier helped a Di comrade register; the sick man lay with his eyes closed, unable to wake.

Asked whose relative he was, the Qiang soldier shook his head. “All I know is that his name is Du. On the day of the river fighting, he carried me onto the bank.” The clerk wrote *fellow soldier* in the appropriate column, paused, and added the Qiang man’s name beside it.

Messengers leaving Luoyang carried dozens of pages of casualty records. The names still unverified were posted outside the government office for families to inquire about. In the distance a band of veterans from the old units huddled around a fire, looking up at the Qin banner above the city gate. One grumbled that this new army had mixed everyone together so thoroughly that a man could scarcely find someone from his own home district. The Qiang soldier heard him and did not argue. He merely tucked the blanket more closely around the sleeping soldier named Du.

After nightfall, the first rolls reached Chang’an. Fu Jian opened the wooden case himself. Attached at the end was a scroll of blank paper, reserved for the living and the dead who had not yet been found. In the flickering lamplight he took up his brush and wrote the date for the next search. He entered no one’s name in their place.
